title.en: Dante in the Dark Wood: The She-Wolves of Mid-Life
title.zh: 但丁入幽暗森林：中年的三猛獸

region.en: Dark wood beneath a sunlit hill, the dream-journey
region.zh: 向陽山下的幽暗森林，夢遊之境

texts.period: Divine Comedy: Inferno, canto 1, c. 1308-1320 (trans. H. F. Cary, 1814)

source.work: The Divine Comedy, trans. Rev. H. F. Cary, Inferno canto 1

summary.en: Lost in the middle of life, Dante meets the three beasts — the spotted leopard of lust, the lion of pride, the gaunt she-wolf of avarice that 'makes the mountains tremble' — and the shade of Virgil, sent by Beatrice, who offers the guided passage through Hell and Purgatory to the stars. The Comedy's frame-poem: everyman's mid-life crisis turned into the West's master-journey of the soul.
summary.zh: 人生中途迷途的但丁遇三獸——斑斕的豹、雄獅、以及「令群山顫抖」的瘦母狼——並遇奉貝雅特麗齊之命而來的維吉爾之影，允諾引其穿越地獄與煉獄，直至繁星。全詩框架由此立定：常人的中年危機化作西方靈魂之旅的總綱。

sensitivity.note: Christian literary-religious imagination (not scripture); presented as comparative underworld-journey narrative.

passages.text: In the midway of this our mortal life, I found me in a gloomy wood, astray gone from the path direct: and e'en to tell it were no easy task, how savage wild that forest, how robust and rough its growth, which to remember only, my dismay renews, in bitterness not far from death. But when a mountain's foot I reach'd, where clos'd the valley, that had pierc'd my heart with dread, I look'd aloft, and saw his shoulders broad already vested with that planet's beam, who leads all wanderers safe through every way.

My weary frame after short pause recomforted, I again took the road, and left the steep, plucking the sloping brake with foremost foot, till at a hole in the valley I arriv'd whose dreadful thrills would render vain my verse. And poison'd without humour of a god, my good Virgil with gentle accents moved me to the view, and bade me behold the three that came in sight: the spotted panther, the lion that did make my flesh to tremble, and the famish'd she-wolf, that of all losses most appals the man who wins.

Then the courteous spirit answered me: Thou shalt not make thy passage without me; for the road I take is round about the mountain that bars thee from the shining height of thy dear home. And I: What needeth me to go? And he: Thou shalt indeed go, and yet not of thyself; for thou art one whose path is held in fee by him, who by his wisdom shall be thy guide through every place thou hast to see. The she-wolf makes the mountains tremble; and the man whom thou must follow by long experience, till he place thee in the sight of her, whose beauty hath such power, that she shall be thine aidance through the darkest and most rugged path.

title.en: The Gate of Hell and the Souls That Lived Without Disgrace and Without Praise
title.zh: 地獄之門與「無譽無辱」的靈魂

region.en: Hell's gate, fore-courts of the abyss

texts.period: Divine Comedy: Inferno, canto 3, c. 1308-1320 (trans. H. F. Cary, 1814)

source.work: The Divine Comedy, trans. Rev. H. F. Cary, Inferno canto 3

summary.en: The gate's inscription — 'Through me you pass into the city of woe... All hope abandon ye who enter here' — opens the Comedy's most feared geography. Beyond it wail the wretched neutrals, 'who lived without disgrace and without praise', mixed with the angels that sided neither with God nor Satan in the rebellion, following a banner that never stops: 'let us not speak of them, but look, and pass on.' At Acheron, Charon the demon boatman threatens the living passenger who will not ride in the dark bark.
summary.zh: 門上銘文——「由我這裏，直通悲慘之城……入此門者，當捨棄一切希望」——開啟全詩最可怖的地域。門內哀號者是被斥為「一生無譽亦無辱」的騎牆者，與叛天時既不從神亦不從撒但的天使同列，追隨一面永不停歇的旗幟——「莫談他們，且看且行」。阿刻戎河上，惡鬼船夫卡戎恐嚇不肯乘上黑舟的活客。

sensitivity.note: Christian literary-religious imagination; the gate inscription is among the West's most quoted lines.

passages.text: Through me you pass into the city of woe: through me you pass into eternal pain: through me among the people lost for aye. Justice the founder of my fabric mov'd: to rear me was the task of power divine, supremest wisdom, and primeval love. Before me things create were none, save things eternal, and eternal I endure. All hope abandon ye who enter here.

Then I look'd round me and beheld, on each side of me, extended in long array, a troop of souls, that seem'd without all hope. With straining eyes, we then gaz'd on a bough which never should have left its parent stem; and, from amid that multitude, innumerable, who had not part in glory, 'let us not speak of them, but look, and pass on,' thus spake my master, 'without disgrace and without praise they lived.'

And now the foul boat skimming the bank at last approaches, with a ghastly demon, a ferryman, Who all asunder tore me from their griefs: And bore me to the bark, and cried to the gathered souls: 'Go where the rest, eternal and for evermore, await your doom.' And like to autumn leaves, that one by one fall and are still, upon the bosom of the stream the guilty seeds of Adam's race, that once were told of, now departing, wait upon the sign, and fall one after other in the stream, as little birds at winter's season rush to land, all on their migration bent, when they must cross.

title.en: Limbo: The Great Souls Who Served Not God Aright
title.zh: 靈薄獄：未曾正確事奉神的偉大靈魂

texts.period: Divine Comedy: Inferno, canto 4, c. 1308-1320 (trans. H. F. Cary, 1814)

source.work: The Divine Comedy, trans. Rev. H. F. Cary, Inferno canto 4

summary.en: No torment but eternal sighing 'not caus'd by tortures, but from grief felt by those multitudes' — the unbaptized of every age, where Virgil himself dwells: 'For these defects, and for no other evil, we are lost; only so far afflicted, that we live desiring without hope.' Dante meets Homer, Horace, Ovid, and Lucan, the philosophers, and the towered noble castle of the great souls of antiquity, amid whom he is a sixth amid so much worth.
summary.zh: 此處無刑罰，只有永遠的歎息——「非因折磨，乃因悲傷」——即歷代未受洗者之群，維吉爾本人亦在其中：「因這些缺失，而非別的罪惡，我們滅亡；所受的苦，只是無望而活著渴想。」但丁在此遇荷馬、賀拉斯、奧維德與盧坎，並入先賢名哲的高貴城堡，置身「如此多英靈之中，我居第六位」。

sensitivity.note: Christian literary imagination; Limbo (limbus patrum/infantium) is a contested doctrine Dante crystallizes.

passages.text: Here, as mine ear could note, no plaint was heard except of sighs, that made th' eternal air tremble, not caus'd by tortures, but from grief felt by those multitudes, many and vast, of men, women, and infants. Then to me the gentle guide: Inquir'st thou not what spirits are these, which thou beholdest? Ere thou pass farther, I would thou know, that these of sin were blameless; and if aught they merited, it profits not, since baptism was not theirs, the portal to thy faith. If they before the Gospel liv'd, they serv'd not God aright; and among such am I.

For these defects, and for no other evil, we are lost; only so far afflicted, that we live desiring without hope. So grief assail'd my heart at hearing this, for well I knew suspended in that Limbo many a soul of mighty worth. Then turning to him I said: Master, enter and search the limits of this realm, and I thy guiding next will follow. Behold the noble castle of those worthies, and passing o'er the gate, within whose bounds he said, We stood: where in a meadow fair, of fresh green herbage, there were met together the spirits of mighty men.

Onward he moved, and I before him walk'd; and of the noblest of the fellowship he made me hear and see: Homer the sovereign bard of old, Horace the satirist, Ovid, and Lucan; and more beside, than mine own prudence can recount, in concert at that noble self, made me a sixth amid so much wisdom. Thus we fared onward to the light, discoursing things of which silence is as well become as speech, while on the sunny mountain top we stray'd.

title.en: Francesca and Paolo: No Greater Grief Than to Remember Days of Joy
title.zh: 弗蘭切斯卡與保羅：無痛過於憶樂

region.en: Second circle of Hell, storm of lust

texts.period: Divine Comedy: Inferno, canto 5, c. 1308-1320 (trans. H. F. Cary, 1814)

source.work: The Divine Comedy, trans. Rev. H. F. Cary, Inferno canto 5

summary.en: In the black whirlwind of the carnal sinners, two souls ride the storm together; Francesca da Rimini tells how she and her husband's brother Paolo read 'of Lancelot, how love impell'd him to her', and at one point alone — 'that day we read no more.' Dante, who at the end faints 'as a dead body falls', asks Minos and the wind-swept how pity so assails him. 'No greater grief than to remember days of joy, when mis'ry is at hand!' — the West's supreme pity-laden love tragedy.
summary.zh: 在肉慾者的黑旋風中，兩靈同行同風；弗蘭切斯卡敘述她與夫弟保羅共讀「蘭斯洛特如何為愛所驅」，讀至「那一日我們再沒有往下讀」。但丁終至如死屍般昏倒。全詩中最哀傷的一問：「處在苦難之中，回憶快樂之日，豈有比這更大的悲傷！」——西方文學至高的憐憫愛情悲劇。

sensitivity.note: Christian literary imagination; adultery presented within the poem's moral geography — pity coexists with judgment.

passages.text: Now 'gin the rueful wailings to be heard. Now am I come where many a plaining voice smites on mine ear. Into a place I came where light was silent all. Bellowing there groan'd a noise as of a sea in tempest torn by warring winds. The stormy blast of hell with restless fury drives the spirits on, whirl'd round and dash'd amain with sore annoy. I understood that to this torment sad the carnal sinners are condemn'd, in whom reason by lust is sway'd.

Soon as the wind in our favour blew, I spake: O wearied spirits! come, and hold discourse with us, by which and whom, if none deny it, the poor garment that I wear shall have peace till the end. The gentler of the twain began: O courteous and benignant spirit! who vouchsafest to question us, and to hear our wailings, we were of the kingdom of the Lombards, and both were lovers, and we read the tale of Lancelot, how love impell'd him to her. When we had read how the fond smile was kiss'd by such a lover, he, who from me shall never be divorced, kiss'd my mouth all trembling.

The book and writer both were love's purveyors. In its leaves that day we read no more. While the one spirit said this, the other wept so sorely, that I for pity swoon'd away, as if I had been dying, and fell down even as a dead body falls.

Thouarest, Francesca, thy sad tale, as hearts do share grief where they feel it near. But if thou hast the will to hear more of our misery, I will tell thee whence we came: No greater grief than to remember days of joy, when mis'ry is at hand! That kens thy great instructor, though he teach not thus in verse, he wrote so faithfully. But if thou hast the will, do ask us more. That day we read no more. As I stood there and listen'd, I was rapt in thought; and when the rest had pass'd, he of the courteous bearing, and the gentle one that was with him, cried out together to me: Lead, Master! we entreat thee, quickly; and the time of thy converse we request.

region.zh: 地獄第七環，自戕者之林

texts.period: Divine Comedy: Inferno, canto 13, c. 1308-1320 (trans. H. F. Cary, 1814)

source.work: The Divine Comedy, trans. Rev. H. F. Cary, Inferno canto 13

summary.en: A thorn-forest of dusky foliage, thick with harpies who wail on the branches — for the self-destroyers are turned to plants, to be plucked at judgment and never wear again their own flesh. Dante breaks a twig and blood runs down as the trunk cries 'Why pluck'st thou me? Men once were we, that now are rooted here.' Pier della Vigna, Frederick's double-keyed secretary, tells his fall from honour to slanderous disgrace; and from among the trees, where harpies feed, the ghosts of hanged men come running.
summary.zh: 陰鬱的荊棘之林，人面鷹身的哈耳庇埃在枝頭哀鳴——自戕者被化作草木，末日審判時方可復得己肉而永不復得。但丁折斷一根樹枝，血沿樹幹滴落，樹身喊道：「你為何折斷我？我們曾是世人，如今被植於此。」彼特羅·德拉·維尼亞——腓特烈雙鑰的重臣——自述由尊榮墜入讒言之辱；哈耳庇埃啄食的樹間，被吊者的幽靈奔竄而來。

sensitivity.note: Christian literary imagination; the metamorphosis-punishment is Dante's most famous invention against self-destruction.

passages.text: Ere Nessus yet had reach'd the other bank, we enter'd on a forest, where no track of steps had worn a way. Not verdant there the foliage, but of dusky hue; not light the boughs and tapering, but with knares deform'd and matted thick: fruits there were none, but thorns instead, with venom fill'd. Here the brute Harpies make their nest, the same who from the Strophades the Trojan band drove with dire boding of their future woe. Broad are their pennons, of the human form their neck and count'nance, arm'd with talons keen the feet, and the huge belly fledge with wings. These sit and wail on the drear mystic wood.

Thereat a little stretching forth my hand, from a great wilding gather'd I a branch, and straight the trunk exclaim'd: Why pluck'st thou me? Then as the dark blood trickled down its side, these words it added: Wherefore tear'st me thus? Is there no touch of mercy in thy breast? Men once were we, that now are rooted here. Thy hand might well have spar'd us, had we been the souls of serpents. As a brand yet green, that burning at one end from the other sends a groaning sound, and hisses with the wind that forces out its way, so burst at once forth from the broken splinter words and blood.

I it was who held both keys to Frederick's heart, and turn'd, locking and unlocking, with so sweet a strength, that from his privy purpose, few did thrust me. Sleeping and waking I was still so true, that I was as it were another man, since I did trust to my integrity. But that foul envy, which but turns to evil her own most gracious temper, was the cause of all my ruin, infusing such a poison in the emperor's breast, that, drawn from state and honour, I did fall, and from the loftiest height. And then, with those disloyal thoughts, my temper, that was loath'd and hated, and did blush to be accounted vile, my breast did beat, and with a fatal blow upon a tree, my flesh fell from me: and now to the tree, by my own sentence, I have changed my body.

title.en: Ulysses' Last Voyage Beyond the Pillars

region.en: Eighth chasm of Hell, fire-cloaked spirits
region.zh: 地獄第八溝，火焰裹身的靈魂

texts.period: Divine Comedy: Inferno, canto 26, c. 1308-1320 (trans. H. F. Cary, 1814)

source.work: The Divine Comedy, trans. Rev. H. F. Cary, Inferno canto 26

summary.en: In the eighth chasm a single flame, parted at the summit like a tongue, holds Ulysses and Diomede together — punished for the horse, Achilles' guile, and the Palladium. At Virgil's entreaty the greater horn rolls and speaks: leaving Circe, 'nor fondness for my son, nor reverence of my old father... could overcome in me the zeal I had t' explore the world, and search the ways of life, man's evil and his virtue' — past Hercules' pillars, 'O brothers!... ye were not form'd to live the life of brutes, but to follow virtue and knowledge', until the sea closed over them before the mountain of Purgatory.
summary.zh: 第八溝中一支頂端裂如舌頭的火舌，裹著尤利西斯與第奧墨得——馬計、阿基琉斯之詭與帕拉狄翁之罪的刑罰。維吉爾代求後，老火舌開口：辭別瑟西之後，「不為幼子之愛、老父之敬……能勝我探索世界、追尋人生善惡之志」——越過海力克士之柱，「兄弟們啊……你們生來不是為獸類之生，而是要追尋美德與知識」——直到煉獄山前海水合攏。

sensitivity.note: Christian literary imagination; Dante's invented ending of the Odyssey is among the most influential rewritings of Greek myth.

passages.text: The guide, who mark'd how I did gaze attentive, thus began: Within these ardours are the spirits, each swath'd in confining fire. He replied: Within Ulysses there and Diomede endure their penal tortures, thus to vengeance now together hasting, as erewhile to wrath. These in the flame with ceaseless groans deplore the ambush of the horse, that open'd wide a portal for that goodly seed to pass, which sow'd imperial Rome; nor less the guile lament they, whence of her Achilles reft Deidamia yet in death complains. And there is rued the stratagem, that Troy of her Palladium spoil'd.

Of the old flame forthwith the greater horn began to roll, murmuring, as a fire that labours with the wind, then to and fro wagging the top, as a tongue uttering sounds, threw out its voice, and spake: When I escap'd from Circe, who beyond a circling year had held me near Caieta, by her charms, ere thus Aeneas yet had nam'd the shore, nor fondness for my son, nor reverence of my old father, nor return of love, that should have crown'd Penelope with joy, could overcome in me the zeal I had t' explore the world, and search the ways of life, man's evil and his virtue. Forth I sail'd into the deep illimitable main, with but one bark, and the small faithful band that yet cleav'd to me.

Tardy with age were I and my companions, when we came to the strait pass, where Hercules ordain'd the bound'ries not to be o'erstepp'd by man. The walls of Seville to my right I left, on the other hand already Ceuta past. O brothers! I began, who to the west through perils without number now have reach'd, to this the short remaining vigil of your senses still be true, that ye may not, in the wheel of your own five glad senses, deny experience of the unpeopled world behind the sun. Consider of your origin: ye were not form'd to live the life of brutes, but to follow virtue and knowledge. Five times re-illum'd, as oft vanish'd, from beneath the moon, the light that had been ours, was spent, when the strait of the true sea-gate we enter'd.

Then of our tall mast we rear'd, we spread the sail, gave way, and travell'd the flood; and more and more to larboard we did turn. 'T was the end of night, the stars already far, that rose when we first parted from the sea, and their companions fled with such a flight of east wind; and ere then a mountain rose up, to us new made, as in the shapes of those that so far appear'd to us; we joy'd, but soon to mourning turn'd; for from the new land a whirlwind rose, and smote our ship; the waves, that follow'd, bore away her poop; and o'er our heads the bow, with both her men, and all our weight of lives, was cast; and thrice turn'd round with all the waters, at the fifth arose, and sank our vessel, and the sea clos'd over as it pleas'd another.

title.zh: 烏哥利諾伯爵的饑餓之塔

region.zh: 地獄第九環，冰封科塞特斯（比薩）

texts.period: Divine Comedy: Inferno, canto 33, c. 1308-1320 (trans. H. F. Cary, 1814)

source.work: The Divine Comedy, trans. Rev. H. F. Cary, Inferno canto 33

summary.en: In the ice of traitors, Count Ugolino gnaws the skull of Archbishop Ruggieri, who imprisoned him. His tale: locked with his sons in the Tower of Famine, he dreams the hunt that gored wolf and whelps, wakes to hear his boys weep for bread, and 'all stone I felt within' will not weep before them. 'Father, we should grieve far less, if thou wouldst eat of us' — and after days of silence, hunger does what grief could not. Pisa's shame is thundered in the comedy's most harrowing canto.
summary.zh: 叛徒之冰中，烏哥利諾伯爵啃咬囚他入塔的呂吉埃里主教之顱。他的故事：與諸子同鎖「饑餓之塔」，夢見狼與幼狼被獵犬咬傷，醒來聽孩子哭討麵包；「我心中如石，不肯在他們面前流淚」。「父親啊，你若吃了我們，我們的悲痛便會小得多」——靜默數日後，饑餓做了悲傷做不到的事。這是全詩最令人心碎的一章，比薩之恥被雷鳴般宣告。

sensitivity.note: Christian literary imagination; the child deaths are within the poem's judgment frame and recounted with horror, not endorsed.

passages.text: His jaws uplifting from their fell repast, that sinner wip'd them on the hairs o' th' head, which he behind had mangled, then began: Thy will obeying, I call up afresh sorrow past cure, which but to think of wrings my heart, or ere I tell on't. Know I was on earth Count Ugolino, and th' Archbishop he Ruggieri. Why I neighbour him so close, now list. That through effect of his ill thoughts in him my trust reposing, I was ta'en and after murder'd, need is not I tell. What therefore thou canst not have heard, that is, how cruel was the murder, shalt thou hear, and know if he have wrong'd me.

When I awoke before the dawn, amid their sleep I heard my sons (for they were with me) weep and ask for bread. Right cruel art thou, if no pang thou feel at thinking what my heart foretold. Now had they waken'd; and the hour drew near when they were wont to bring us food; the mind of each misgave him through his dream, and I heard, at its outlet underneath lock'd up the horrible tower: whence uttering not a word I look'd upon the visage of my sons. I wept not: so all stone I felt within. They wept: and one, my little Anslem, cried: Thou lookest so! Father what ails thee? Yet I shed no tear, nor answer'd all that day nor the next night, until another sun came out upon the world.

When a faint beam had to our doleful prison made its way, and in four countenances I descry'd the image of my own, on either hand through agony I bit, and they who thought I did it through desire of feeding, rose o' th' sudden, and cried, Father, we should grieve far less, if thou wouldst eat of us: thou gav'st these weeds of miserable flesh we wear, and do thou strip them off from us again. Then, not to make them sadder, I kept down my spirit in stillness. That day and the next we all were silent. Ah, obdurate earth! Why open'dst not thy gates for us?

The fourth day came, and Gaddo at my feet fell outstretched. What more thou hast to ask, or wherefore have I strength? What more hast thou to ask, or why my tongue longer speak? We were four souls; I gave my life a prey to hunger and to grief, or e'en the sixth day's sun had reached its meridian height; my sons who perish'd in the tower, Pisa, had I not murdered them, thou knowest the story well: 'twas my own flesh they wanted. Then I, where I had been, still sought; and neither dead nor living, I or they knew more. And in my grief, that quiet sleepless grief, I did not move; but lay and rooted in the ice of my great sorrow.

title.en: The Three-Faced Lucifer in the Frozen Lake

region.en: Ninth circle, well of Cocytus, centre of the earth
region.zh: 地獄第九環，科塞特斯冰湖，大地中心

texts.period: Divine Comedy: Inferno, canto 34, c. 1308-1320 (trans. H. F. Cary, 1814)

source.work: The Divine Comedy, trans. Rev. H. F. Cary, Inferno canto 34

summary.en: At the bottom of the universe Lucifer, 'the creature eminent in beauty once', stands fixed in ice — three faces, bat-like wings whose flapping freezes Cocytus with three winds, six eyes weeping bloody foam, and three mouths chewing Judas, Brutus, and Cassius. The geography is geometry's: the climbers emerge 'to see again the stars' on the far hemisphere, having crossed the center of the earth — for Hell was made when Heaven fled from Lucifer, 'the earth that sway'd him, he did raise from fear' of the sun.
summary.zh: 宇宙之底，昔日「容顏絕倫」的魯西弗倒嵌於冰中——三面、蝙蝠之翼（其撲動以三股風凍結科塞特斯）、六眼滴血淚，三口咀嚼猶大、布魯圖與卡修斯。地理即是幾何：二人穿過地心，「再度看見繁星」於另一半天球——因為當諸天從魯西弗遁逃時，地獄便在其落點生成了。

sensitivity.note: Christian literary imagination; the frozen-Lucifer geography is Dante's own invention, not scriptural.

passages.text: The banners of Hell's Monarch do come forth towards us; therefore look, so spake my guide, if thou discern him. As, when breathes a cloud heavy and dense, or when the shades of night fall on our hemisphere, seems view'd from far a windmill, which the blast stirs briskly round, such was the fabric then methought I saw. Now came I (and with fear I bid my strain record the marvel) where the souls were all whelm'd underneath, transparent, as through glass pellucid the frail stem.

That emperor, who sways the realm of sorrow, at mid breast from th' ice stood forth. That creature, whose appearance was once most beauteous, as he is hideous now, and yet did dare to scowl upon his Maker, well from him may all our mis'ry flow. How passing strange it seem'd, when I did spy upon his head three faces: one in front of hue vermilion, th' other two with this midway each shoulder join'd and at the crest. Under each shot forth two mighty wings, enormous as became a bird so vast. No plumes had they, but were in texture like a bat, and these he flapp'd i' th' air, that from him issued still three winds, wherewith Cocytus to its depth was frozen. At six eyes he wept: the tears adown three chins distill'd with bloody foam.

At every mouth his teeth a sinner champ'd bruis'd as with pond'rous engine, so that three were in this guise tormented. That upper spirit, who hath worse punishment, so spake my guide, is Judas, he that hath his head within and plies the feet without. Of th' other two, whose heads are under, from the murky jaw who hangs, is Brutus: lo! how he doth writhe and speaks not! Th' other Cassius, that appears so large of limb. And noting how that Lucifer had three winds for the frozen river, they departed; till my guide, within the hollow cave whose floor already stank, that led us back to the fair world, set me upon the steep, and first himself descended the rough bank; I following his steps, we climbed, he first, I following his steps, till on our view the beautiful lights of heav'n dawn'd through a circular opening in the cave: thus issuing we again beheld the stars.

title.en: Virgil Departs: Come, Spouse, from Libanus
title.zh: 維吉爾離去：新婦，自黎巴嫩而來

texts.period: Divine Comedy: Purgatorio, canto 30, c. 1308-1320 (trans. H. F. Cary, 1814)

source.work: The Divine Comedy, trans. Rev. H. F. Cary, Purgatorio canto 30

summary.en: At the top of Purgatory, where the thorn forest of the earthly Paradise blooms, Beatrice descends in a shower of white-veiled flowers 'beneath green mantle, rob'd in hue of living flame' — and Virgil, reason's guide, is gone: 'Virgil had bereav'd us of himself, Virgil, my best-lov'd father... nor all, our prime mother lost, avail'd to save my undew'd cheeks from blur of soiling tears.' Beatrice's rebuke opens the second half of the Comedy: 'Dante, weep not, that Virgil leaves thee... behooves thee feel the edge of other sword.'
summary.zh: 煉獄山頂的地上樂園中，貝雅特麗齊在白色花雨中降臨——「著綠色斗篷，披火焰之色」——而理性的導師維吉爾已離去：「維吉爾，我至愛的父親，捨我而去……縱大地之母盡失，也未能拭去我臉上的淚痕。」貝雅特麗齊的斥責開啟全詩下半：「但丁，莫為維吉爾之去而哭泣……你還須感到另一柄劍的鋒刃。」

sensitivity.note: Christian literary imagination; the classical guide replaced by the theological one is the Comedy's structural argument.

passages.text: Forthwith the saintly tribe, who in the van between the Gryphon and its radiance came, did turn them to the car, as to their rest: and one, as if commission'd from above, in holy chant thrice shorted forth aloud: Come, spouse, from Libanus! and all the rest took up the song. I have beheld, ere now, at break of day, the eastern clime all roseate, and the sky oppos'd, one deep and beautiful serene, and the sun's face so shaded, and with mists attemper'd at lids rising, that the eye long while endur'd the sight: thus in a cloud of flowers, that from those hands angelic rose, and down, within and outside of the car, fell showering, in white veil with olive wreath'd, a virgin in my view appear'd, beneath green mantle, rob'd in hue of living flame.

No sooner on my vision streaming, smote the heav'nly influence, which years past, and e'en in childhood, thrill'd me, than towards Virgil I turn'd me to leftward, panting, like a babe, that flees for refuge to his mother's breast, if aught have terrified or work'd him woe: and would have cried: There is no dram of blood, that doth not quiver in me. The old flame throws out clear tokens of reviving fire: but Virgil had bereav'd us of himself, Virgil, my best-lov'd father; Virgil, he to whom I gave me up for safety: nor, all, our prime mother lost, avail'd to save my undew'd cheeks from blur of soiling tears. Dante, weep not, that Virgil leaves thee: nay, weep thou not yet: behooves thee feel the edge of other sword, and thou shalt weep for that.

title.en: The Love That Moves the Sun and All the Stars

texts.period: Divine Comedy: Paradiso, canto 33, c. 1308-1320 (trans. H. F. Cary, 1814)

source.work: The Divine Comedy, trans. Rev. H. F. Cary, Paradiso canto 33

summary.en: The Comedy's close: St Bernard prays to the Virgin — 'O virgin mother, daughter of thy Son... Here kneeleth one, who of all spirits hath review'd the state, from the world's lowest gap unto this height' — and Dante's sight, refined, passes into 'the ray authentical of sovran light', where 'in one volume clasp'd of love, whatever the universe unfolds' is seen: three orbs of triple hue, 'as rainbow is from rainbow.' The last line of the poem is the doctrine: 'But yet the will roll'd onward, like a wheel in even motion, by the Love impell'd, that moves the sun in heav'n and all the stars.'
summary.zh: 全詩收束：聖伯爾納向童貞女祈求——「童貞女母，聖子之女……此人閱盡靈界，自世界最低之淵至此至高之光」——但丁的目光被煉淨，進入「至聖之光的真實之射線」，其中「以愛裝訂成一冊，收錄宇宙所展開的一切」：三環三色，「如虹出自虹」。全詩末行即是教義：「然而意志卻如均勻轉動的車輪，由那推動太陽與群星之愛所驅。」

sensitivity.note: Christian literary imagination; the Marian intercession is doctrinal poetry, not scripture.

passages.text: O virgin mother, daughter of thy Son, created beings all in lowliness surpassing, as in height, above them all, term by th' eternal counsel pre-ordain'd, ennobler of thy nature, so advanc'd in thee, that its great Maker did not scorn, himself, in his own work enclos'd to dwell! For in thy womb rekindling shone the love reveal'd, whose genial influence makes now this flower to germin in eternal peace! Here kneeleth one, who of all spirits hath review'd the state, from the world's lowest gap unto this height. Suppliant to thee he kneels, imploring grace for virtue, yet more high to lift his ken toward the bliss supreme.

The eyes, that heav'n with love and awe regards, fix'd on the suitor, witness'd, how benign she looks on pious pray'rs: then fasten'd they on th' everlasting light, wherein no eye of creature, as may well be thought, so far can travel inward. I, meanwhile, who drew near to the limit, where all wishes end, the ardour of my wish (for so behooved), ended within me. Bare me into the ray authentical of sovran light. Thenceforward, what I saw, was not for words to speak, nor memory's self to stand against such outrage on her skill.

O grace! unenvying of thy boon! that gav'st boldness to fix so earnestly my ken on th' everlasting splendour, that I look'd, while sight was unconsum'd, and, in that depth, saw in one volume clasp'd of love, whatever the universe unfolds; all properties of substance and of accident, beheld, compounded, yet one individual light the whole. In that abyss of radiance, clear and lofty, seem'd methought, three orbs of triple hue clipt in one bound: and, from another, one reflected seem'd, as rainbow is from rainbow: and the third seem'd fire, breath'd equally from both. Here vigour fail'd the tow'ring fantasy: but yet the will roll'd onward, like a wheel in even motion, by the Love impell'd, that moves the sun in heav'n and all the stars.
